L0@P0: NOVEMBER 2000
L1@P0-1: GAME DEVELOPER MAGAZINEGAME PLAN
L2@P1: ✎
L3@P1: LETTER FROM THE EDITOR
L4@P1: Nearly four and a half years
L5@P1: ago, Alex Dunne first
L6@P1: appeared in this space. Four
L7@P1: and a half years! That’s a
L8@P1: long time to be doing anything, even more so in our industry, where
L9@P1: it’s rare to be working on something for
L10@P1: longer than two years (well, except for a
L11@P1: few games!). To give you a sense of perspective, in that issue of Game Developer
L12@P1: DirectX 2 was highlighted. At the Computer Game Developers Conference that
L13@P1: year, Intel announced MMX, 3Dfx
L14@P1: announced the Voodoo graphics chipset,
L15@P1: and Apple announced Game Sprockets.
L16@P1: Doesn’t that seem like a long time ago?
L17@P1: Many things have changed during these
L18@P1: years, but you could always depend on
L19@P1: Alex and Game Developer. Month after
L20@P1: month, Alex gave readers insight into our
L21@P1: industry, pointed out the shadowy nooks
L22@P1: and crannies, and guided developers over
L23@P1: bumps such as software patents. Alex
L24@P1: didn’t just point out industry issues, he created things like the Independent Games
L25@P1: Festival, an annual showcase for independently developed games.
L26@P1: It is with sadness that we bid Alex goodbye, but of course he hasn’t gone very far.
L27@P1: Alex is now the executive producer for our
L28@P1: sister publication, Gamasutra.com, and I’m
L29@P1: sure he’ll bring to that forum the same discerning eye for what’s important to you.
L30@P1: Enter, Stage Right
L31@P1: So you may be wondering, who is this
L32@P1: guy, and what’s he doing here? Hi, I’m
L33@P1: Mark DeLoura, the new editor-in-chief for
L34@P1: Game Developer. Like many of you, I’ve
L35@P1: worked at numerous places, but my primary gig for the past five years has been as
L36@P1: software engineering lead at Nintendo of
L37@P1: America. While at Nintendo, I was the key
L38@P1: Nintendo 64 developer relations person,
L39@P1: and I wrote the November 1999 article on
L40@P1: rendering Bézier surfaces using N64 microcode. For the last year and a half I’ve led a
L41@P1: team of brilliant software engineers, working on demos and libraries for Nintendo’s
L42@P1: Gamecube and Game Boy Advance.
L43@P1: My background prior to working at
L44@P1: Nintendo includes a heavy dose of virtual
L45@P1: reality and an arcade game that never
L46@P1: shipped. I spent quite a few years working
L47@P1: with virtual reality at the Human Interface
L48@P1: Technology Lab and UNC-Chapel Hill,
L49@P1: and I co-moderated the Usenet newsgroup
L50@P1: sci.virtual-worlds. Then there was the
L51@P1: whole networked multiplayer arcade game
L52@P1: thing, which sounded like a great idea, and
L53@P1: did actually work as long as you ran it on
L54@P1: a $250,000 SGI Onyx.
L55@P1: Most recently I organized and edited the
L56@P1: book Game Programming Gems, which is
L57@P1: a collection of programming tips and tricks
L58@P1: from 40 professional game developers.
L59@P1: (And yes, that would be a shameless plug!)
L60@P1: Engage
L61@P1: Where are we going from here? It’s an
L62@P1: incredibly exciting and challenging
L63@P1: time to be a game developer. In the console
L64@P1: space we’re faced with four very different
L65@P1: platforms to work on: porting games
L66@P1: between them is going to be ugly. On the
L67@P1: PC side, the range of performance you now
L68@P1: must account for demands scalability and
L69@P1: hardcore bug-testing. Handheld gaming is
L70@P1: launching into completely new areas, with
L71@P1: cellular communication, four-player multiplay and console-handheld connectivity.
L72@P1: And then there’s web gaming, persistent
L73@P1: worlds, and the mod community. So we
L74@P1: certainly have a lot of material to cover!
L75@P1: It’s clear that having a resource to help
L76@P1: you make decisions about your games is
L77@P1: valuable. We’re pleased that one resource
L78@P1: you’ve chosen is Game Developer magazine. Our commitment to providing timely,
L79@P1: innovative material is unwavering. We plan
L80@P1: to broaden our coverage of many types of
L81@P1: gaming, as interactive entertainment continues its transition from a niche activity to a
L82@P1: truly mass-market art form. These next few
L83@P1: years are going to be a doozy!
L84@P1: Sunset, Sunrise
L85@P1: CLet us know what you think. Send
L86@P1: e-mail to editors@gdmag.com, or write

L18: Rogue, published in 1980, is the game that established the genre and inspired all other Roguelikes.
L19: ## Description
L20: 
L21: Rogue's storyline was very light: the point of the game was to go down all levels of a 【26†dungeon】, in a world based on 【9†Dungeons & Dragons】, starting from the top, killing monsters and plundering treasures, until finding the 【27†Amulet of Yendor】. Then, the player had to climb every level up.
L22: It was one of the first games to use a spatial representation of the world where the action unfolded instead of textual descriptions - the authors sought to combine a traditional "dice" RPG with the original Crowther/Woods 【28†interactive fiction】 game 【10†Colossal Cave Adventure】. This was possible using a 【17†C】 function library called 【29†Curses】, and this brought important advancements into the cRPG and in general PC gaming genre.
L23: Contrary to many other computer RPGs of the time, all levels were 【30†randomly generated】. Rogue was intended to be played on Unix terminals. Thus, the dungeon was displayed in text mode, characters and monsters being represented by letters. Actions were issued by single keystrokes. Rogue defined the very Roguelike genre. Random generation, basic plot, text (or tiled) based display still are the usual features of Roguelikes.
L24: The more direct descendant of Rogue was 【31†Hack】, although 【32†Larn】 and 【33†Moria】 are closely related to it as well.
L25: ## Versions and platforms
L26: 
L27: Rogue was written in 1980 by 【3†Michael Toy】, 【4†Glenn Wichman】 and 【5†Ken Arnold】 for Unix. It was ported to several platforms.
L28: 
L29: Rogue clones can now be found for nearly every existing platform. Notable modern examples include:
